feature: Cut a piece onto its own layer and heal behind it
summary: Draw a marquee round something in a picture, press Shift Command J, and that piece lifts onto a layer of its own while the space it came from fills back in with the colours that were around it. Drag the piece away and what it came off still looks whole, instead of showing a hole or a second copy of the same thing underneath.
setup: Photonz Dev, Experiments window, release Next. The flag is "Cut a piece onto its own layer and heal behind it" and it is on by default. The row is in the Layer menu directly under New Layer via Copy.

try.do: Open a screenshot, pick it, take the marquee (M) and draw a box snug round a heading or a button.
Press V and drag the new layer right off the screenshot.
Zoom into where the piece used to be and look for a seam, a smudge or a ghost of it.
Press Command Z once and check the piece, the hole and the fill all come back together.
Take the ellipse marquee or the wand, select something round or irregular, and press Shift Command J again.
Try it over a busy photograph, where nothing around the piece is one colour or an even ramp.
Draw a rectangle, marquee half of it, and press Shift Command J over that.

evaluate: Shift Command J is Photoshop's key for this exact command, Layer Via Cut, and it sits under New Layer via Copy which is its twin. You asked for Command Shift X. Is the Photoshop key the right call here, or do you want the one you named?

When nothing around the piece agrees, it still cuts and fills with the middle colour of what was around it, and the pill says the fill was a guess. Is cutting anyway right, or would you rather it refused and left the picture alone?
Nothing is said at all when the fill was read cleanly off the picture. Is that the right amount of quiet, or do you want to know every time?

The new layer is named the way duplicating that layer names it, so a piece of "Photonz drop probe" is called "Photonz drop probe 2". Does that read right in the layers list for a piece, or should a piece be named for itself?
The piece keeps nothing of the layer it came off: a blur or a shadow on the screenshot stays on the screenshot. Is that what you expect?
rough: THE KEY. You asked for Command Shift X. This shipped on Shift Command J instead, because that is Photoshop's own key for this exact command, Command Shift X is Photoshop's Liquify, and the row belongs directly under New Layer via Copy which is the same command without the healing. Your standing rule is to default new keys to Photoshop's, so this followed it rather than asking and stalling the feature. It is one line to change if you would rather have the key you named. The two must not both be bound.

WHAT IT FILLS WITH WHEN IT CANNOT READ THE BACKGROUND, and why. The reading has three outcomes. Where the ring around the piece agrees with itself, the space comes back exactly that colour, byte for byte, which is the common case on real UI. Where it ramps evenly, a matching ramp goes in. Where it does neither, the app cannot justify anything, and the answer here is the opposite of what Separate into Layers does: that command picked the piece itself so it skips it, but here a person picked the piece and pressed a key, so refusing would be ignoring an instruction. It cuts, fills with the median colour of the ring, one flat tone so a guess does not pretend to detail it does not have, and the pill says the fill was a guess. The one case with no colour at all is a marquee round the whole layer: there is no background left to read, so the space is left honestly empty.

The ring skips the band of pixels touching the marquee, and reads two to four pixels out. Without that a wand selection, which follows the ink exactly, reads its own antialiased rim as background: a tenth of a white letter is 25 levels off the panel colour, twelve times the tolerance the exact case runs at, so a panel that should come back exact came back as a guess instead.

The layer the piece came off keeps its box and its size. The space was filled, not removed, so there are no fewer pixels to tighten to. That is a difference from Backspace over the same marquee, which shrinks the layer to what survives, and it means the locked Background needs no special handling here at all.

Antialiased edge, and it is the same one Photoshop has. On a soft-edged marquee, an ellipse or a wand, the fill goes in at the marquee's own coverage, so the single rim pixel is part fill and part what was there. On a hard rectangular marquee there is no rim and the result is exact. Visible only when magnified past about 8x.

The piece comes off the layer's BITMAP, so styling on the source layer, a blur or a shadow, stays with the source and does not travel with the piece. Consistent with what Backspace, the bucket and a region drag already do over the same marquee.

WHAT IT COSTS, and what is still unknown. Measured in a debug test build on a 12 megapixel picture: a small marquee about 80ms, and a marquee shaped like an ellipse over half the whole picture about 1.2 seconds. Debug Swift is many times slower than the release build the app actually ships, and in the real probe app the walk's cut landed with no wait you could feel, but the release cost was not measured. Three things were made much faster on the way here and they are in: the mask is one byte a pixel instead of four, the ring walk finds the outline in the mask's own indices instead of converting every one of five million pixels back and forth, and RegionOps.trimmed now probes each row from both ends instead of reading through the middle of it, which speeds up a region delete on a big picture too. A follow-up is filed to measure the release build and decide whether the big marquee case needs more.

The screenshots are real window captures from the playtest walk Scripts/playtest/cut-onto-its-own-layer-walk.json. The magnified before and after is a crop of the document's own pixels rather than a capture, because a seam is a pixel question and window chrome only gets in the way of it.
